name: Vertical Slice Architecture
when_to_use: Rapidly evolving business features, micro-domains with different complexity, independent feature iteration
avoid_when: Simple CRUD micro-apps, monolithic reporting-only databases
key_components: Feature folders, command/query handlers, co-located DTOs, domain models, slice-specific tests
trade_offs: Duplicate DTOs across slices vs decoupled independence
anti_patterns: Layer-hopping, global generic repositories, shared mutable domain models

name: Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters)
when_to_use: Core business logic must outlive frameworks, persistence, and external APIs
avoid_when: Small utility scripts, simple proxy services, high-throughput streaming with minimal business logic
key_components: Core domain entities, driving ports (inbound interfaces), driven ports (outbound interfaces), adapters
trade_offs: Higher initial boilerplate vs complete infrastructure independence
anti_patterns: Framework annotations inside domain core, leaking ORM entities through ports

name: Modular Monolith
when_to_use: Medium to large systems needing clear domain boundaries without microservice operational overhead
avoid_when: Single-developer prototype apps, distributed systems requiring independent hardware scaling
key_components: Bounded contexts, internal module public APIs, private implementations, module communication bus
trade_offs: In-process call latency vs discipline required to prevent boundary leaks
anti_patterns: Direct cross-module database foreign keys, importing internal module classes

name: Clean / Onion Architecture
when_to_use: Enterprise business applications with rich domain rules requiring strict dependency inversion
avoid_when: CRUD applications, fast throwaway MVPs, stream processing pipelines
key_components: Domain entities, use cases / interactors, interface adapters, frameworks/drivers
trade_offs: High layer indirection and DTO mapping overhead vs strict boundary protection
anti_patterns: Entities leaking to UI, business logic leaking into use-case controllers

name: Microservices
when_to_use: Large organizations (>50 engineers) needing autonomous team deployability and independent scaling
avoid_when: Early-stage startups (<10 engineers), tightly coupled domain models with unclear boundaries
key_components: Autonomous services, API contracts (gRPC/REST), CI/CD pipelines, container orchestration, distributed tracing
trade_offs: Network latency, distributed transaction complexity, operational overhead vs organizational scalability
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith (shared database, synchronous HTTP chains), entity-based microservices

name: Event-Driven Pub/Sub
when_to_use: Decoupled, asynchronous notification across subsystems, broadcast state changes, high-throughput ingest
avoid_when: Synchronous request-response queries, simple CRUD operations requiring immediate read-after-write consistency
key_components: Event producers, message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ), event channels, event consumers
trade_offs: Eventual consistency, out-of-order delivery vs massive throughput and loose temporal coupling
anti_patterns: Spaghetti event chains with no central topology, unversioned event payloads

name: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
when_to_use: Read and write workloads have radically different models, performance needs, or scaling characteristics
avoid_when: Standard CRUD applications with balanced reads and writes
key_components: Command model (mutations/validation), Query model (denormalized read projections), Event publisher
trade_offs: Eventual consistency overhead vs optimized read/write performance
anti_patterns: Applying CQRS to the entire application rather than specific bounded contexts

name: Event Sourcing
when_to_use: Systems where complete state history, auditability, temporal querying, or replayability is mandatory (banking, logistics)
avoid_when: Traditional CRUD applications where only current state matters, simple reporting systems
key_components: Append-only event store, aggregate roots, projections/read models, snapshotters
trade_offs: Event schema versioning, projection rebuild latency vs guaranteed audit trail and time travel
anti_patterns: Mutating events in place, treating event stream as transient message queue

name: Transactional Outbox
when_to_use: Guaranteed message publishing in sync with database transactions without two-phase commit (2PC)
avoid_when: Single-node apps with no external asynchronous message consumers
key_components: Outbox table, polling publisher or CDC (e.g. Debezium), message deduplicator, idempotency key
trade_offs: Storage overhead of outbox records vs at-least-once delivery guarantee
anti_patterns: Dual writes to DB and message broker without atomicity, publishing before commit

name: Saga (Orchestrated)
when_to_use: Complex multi-step transactions across independent services with compensating actions
avoid_when: Simple two-step transactions, monolithic single-database operations
key_components: Saga orchestrator, state machine, command dispatchers, compensating action handlers
trade_offs: Single orchestrator complexity vs centralized visibility and error recovery
anti_patterns: Missing compensating action handlers, circular saga dependencies

name: Saga (Choreographed)
when_to_use: Lightweight distributed workflows with 2-4 participants where loose coupling is paramount
avoid_when: Complex workflows with >5 steps where tracking overall progress is critical
key_components: Domain event emitters, event listeners, local compensating transactions
trade_offs: Decentralized simplicity vs difficulty in visualizing end-to-end transaction flow
anti_patterns: Spaghetti event chains, unhandled event rejection leading to inconsistent states

name: Pipes and Filters
when_to_use: Sequential data transformation steps (ETL, compilers, audio/image processing, packet filtering)
avoid_when: Interactive request-response web apps with frequent bi-directional state mutations
trade_offs: Message serialization latency vs composability and independent step reusability
anti_patterns: Tight coupling between filter steps, monolithic filters doing multiple transformations

name: Actor Model
when_to_use: Stateful entities with concurrent access, fine-grained lifecycle management (gaming, chat, IoT, telematics)
avoid_when: Stateless web APIs, bulk relational query workloads
key_components: Actors, mailbox/queues, message protocols, actor supervisor hierarchies
trade_offs: Debugging asynchronous message queues vs lock-free concurrent safety
anti_patterns: Sharing mutable state between actors, blocking calls inside actor message handler

name: Strangler Fig
when_to_use: Incrementally migrating a legacy monolith to modern services or clean architecture
avoid_when: Greenfield projects, complete ground-up rewrites with throwaway legacy code
key_components: API gateway / interceptor proxy, legacy system adapter, modern micro-service/slice
trade_offs: Routing layer latency vs zero-downtime, low-risk phased replacement
anti_patterns: Never finishing the migration, maintaining dual systems indefinitely without deprecation plan

name: API Gateway / BFF (Backend-for-Frontend)
when_to_use: Aggregating multiple internal microservices into client-specific contracts (mobile vs web vs public)
avoid_when: Single monolith backends, internal service-to-service communication
key_components: Gateway reverse proxy, client-specific adapters, rate limiters, auth termination, response aggregators
trade_offs: Single point of failure and gateway latency vs tailored client payloads and client-agnostic backend
anti_patterns: Putting business logic into the API gateway (Smart Endpoints / Dumb Pipes violation)

name: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)
when_to_use: Integrating modern domain with legacy systems or third-party vendor APIs without polluting domain model
avoid_when: Greenfield integrations between two systems that already share identical domain models
key_components: Translators/Adapters, facade interfaces, domain-to-legacy mapping DTOs
trade_offs: Additional mapping code and maintenance vs protecting domain model purity
anti_patterns: Directly referencing vendor SDK objects inside core domain services

name: Data Mesh
when_to_use: Decentralized domain-oriented data ownership for analytical data across large enterprise squads
avoid_when: Centralized startups with single data engineer, simple reporting requirements
key_components: Domain data products, federated computational governance, self-serve data platforms
trade_offs: Governance coordination complexity vs team autonomy and eliminated central bottleneck
anti_patterns: Treating raw operational databases as public analytical data products

name: Serverless Event Processing
when_to_use: Bursty, unpredictable, or event-driven compute (webhook processing, file uploads, scheduled jobs)
avoid_when: Steady-state high-throughput workloads, latency-critical operations sensitive to cold starts
key_components: Function triggers, serverless compute (Lambda/Cloud Run), managed state/queues
trade_offs: Cold start latency, vendor lock-in vs zero idle cost and automatic scaling
anti_patterns: Monolithic functions doing 15 operations, chaining multiple lambdas synchronously
